The annual number of deaths caused by hepatitis B virus (HBV) has decreased from 820,000 to 310,000, which corresponds to a reduction in mortality rates from 10 per 100,000 to 4 per 100,000. 2. Similarly, annual deaths from hepatitis C virus (HCV) have declined from 290,000 to 140,000, reducing mortality rates from 5 per 100,000 to 2 per 100,000. 3. The global targets outlined in the 2022–2030 Global Health Sector Strategies (GHSS) serve as a framework for countries to establish their own national targets. 4. These strategies emphasize a person-centered approach, integrating efforts across HIV, sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and viral hepatitis to ensure a comprehensive response. 5. It is essential for all HIV programs to systematically record and report hepatitis-related indicators to monitor progress effectively. 6. The strategies advocate for equitable progress across all populations, ensuring that those most affected or at higher risk are not left behind. 7. Disaggregated data by age, sex, and other population characteristics are necessary to identify disparities among subpopulations and to monitor trends over time. 8. Person-centered monitoring through routine health information systems (HIS) is critical to maintaining the quality of hepatitis care and tracking the care cascade for HBV and HCV among individuals receiving HIV treatment or prevention services. 9. A minimum set of data elements specific to viral hepatitis testing and treatment should be routinely collected and reported within HIV programs. 10. Viral hepatitis data can be gathered from various HIV program settings, including community outreach, HIV testing, care and treatment clinics, and key population programs. 11. Since viral hepatitis data include individuals living with HIV as well as those receiving HIV testing or prevention services (who may have unknown or negative HIV status), disaggregation by HIV status is crucial. 12. Proposed HBV and HCV indicators for routine collection and reporting within HIV programs are based on the 10 core indicators of the monitoring and evaluation (M&E) framework for viral hepatitis and the targets for viral hepatitis elimination. 13. Data collected from these indicators complement other reporting requirements for Member States to the World Health Organization (WHO), such as the Global AIDS Monitoring (GAM) and the Global Reporting System for Hepatitis (GRSH). 14. Women living with HIV have a six-fold higher risk of developing cervical cancer compared to women without HIV, and cervical cancer is classified as an AIDS-defining condition. 15. This elevated risk is due to increased susceptibility to acquiring human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, lower rates of regression of precancerous lesions, faster progression to cancer, and higher recurrence rates after treatment. 16. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) has significantly reduced AIDS-related mortality and increased life expectancy, with over 19 million women estimated to be living with HIV globally in 2019. 17. The proportion of women living with HIV among cervical cancer patients varies widely by region, reflecting differences in HIV prevalence. 18. In regions with high HIV prevalence, such as southern Africa, up to 40% or more of cervical cancer cases are attributable to HIV, compared to less than 5% in countries with lower HIV prevalence. 19. Cervical cancer is diagnosed at a younger average age in women living with HIV compared to HIV-negative women. 20. WHO’s global strategy to eliminate cervical cancer as a public health problem includes the following 2030 targets: 90% of girls fully vaccinated with the HPV vaccine by age 15. 70% of women screened with a high-performance test by ages 35 and 45. 90% of women identified with cervical disease treated appropriately. 21. Countries with high HIV burdens often have the highest cervical cancer rates, necessitating greater efforts to achieve cervical cancer elimination in these settings. 22. WHO has published updated guidelines on cervical cancer screening and treatment, including 16 new and revised recommendations tailored for women living with HIV. 23. These guidelines aim to simplify screening and treatment algorithms while ensuring feasibility and acceptability for both healthcare providers and women accessing these services. 24. Cervical cancer screening and treatment services should be inclusive of transgender men, non-binary individuals, and intersex individuals with a cervix. 25. Additional training and sensitization of healthcare workers and program managers may be required to ensure inclusivity and accessibility for gender-diverse populations. 26. Public health authorities should prioritize increasing awareness, access, and uptake of cervical cancer screening and treatment among these groups. 27. Minimizing loss to follow-up among women screened positive for cervical precancer and ensuring proper management of invasive cancer are critical to reducing cervical cancer morbidity and mortality. 28. Patient registers or electronic medical records for individuals receiving ART can serve as the primary source of information for identifying those who should be screened for cervical cancer. 29. Data elements for cervical cancer screening can be integrated into these records to facilitate reporting of key indicators. 30. In many cases, cervical cancer screening may occur at a different facility from where treatment is provided, requiring strong referral systems and data integration across services. 31. WHO recommends starting cervical cancer screening at age 25 for women living with HIV, with regular screening every 3 to 5 years. 32. Gender categories in data collection should include all gender-diverse individuals with a female reproductive system, while ensuring confidentiality and privacy to prevent misuse of data. 33. Where safety and legal protections are not in place, gender disaggregation may be excluded to protect individuals. 34. WHO emphasizes the importance of privacy, confidentiality, and protections for key populations and other vulnerable groups in data collection and reporting. 35. The recommended priority indicators for cervical cancer screening and treatment among women living with HIV align with WHO’s guidelines and global strategies for cervical cancer prevention and elimination. 36. Standard disaggregation by 5-year age bands starting at age 20 should be included in data collection. 37. All individuals, regardless of gender identity, have the right to equality and non-discrimination in accessing sexual and reproductive healthcare services.
